newsitem.title: USA: AT&T CEO opens door to merger with Baby Bell.
newsitem.headline: AT&T CEO opens door to merger with Baby Bell.

text.p: AT&T Chairman and Chief Executive Robert Allen will lay out the financial and regulatory arguments for a possible merger with a U.S. Baby Bell company in remarks to be delivered in Boston on Tuesday.

In a statement summarizing the speech, Allen opened the door to a possible merger with a Baby Bell operator, but he stopped short of commenting on reports that A&T may merge with SBC Communications Inc.
The combination of long-distance carriers and Bell companies need not be unthinkable, under the right conditions, Allen said.

Allen said AT&T was prepared to go it alone in entering U.S. local telephone markets -- which currently remain dominated by the regional Bell operators -- but that the company was open to options including a combination with a Baby Bell.

Allen said such a merger would have to be pro-competitive. "AT&T would never consider a regional operating company merger that did not advance competition -- both within and beyond the regional company's home territory," he said.
"Nobody knows the difference between 'competitive' and 'non-competitive' better than AT&T," Allen said. "Many of us are reformed monopolists."
Allen said any partnership with a regional Bell would have to make strategic and financial sense and act to enhance competition in local phone markets.

"It would have to add significantly to our top-line revenue by accelerating our penetration of the local service business," he said. "And it would have to contribute to our goal of growing earnings to $5 to $6 a share by 2001."

He was referring to AT&T's statement at a meeting with Wall Street analysts in March that it had a four-year earnings target of $5 to $6, but that near-term financial results would be hurt by huge investments in new markets.

Conceding that "no company can afford to build local networks quickly across the country," he said he has learned that bringing local service to all 50 states is a "very large, very expensive, very time consuming proposition."
Any merger would have to accelerate competition everywhere in the United States, Allen said, "even in the Bell company's own territory."
Allen said he is not fantasizing about reconstituting the former Bell System. "Ma Bell has passed into the Great Beyond," he said. "She is beyond resurrection.

"The combination of long-distance companies and regional operating companies should only be allowed to happen if people have a real choice for local service from real competitors in the regional companies' territories," he said.

The AT&T chairman said some advantages of combining with a regional Bell would include an expanded capital base to invest in local service facilities, faster development of local market competition and the scale necessary to compete with the mega-carriers under formation around the globe.
